title: The Silent Commute Beneath the Bed
artefact:
# The Silent Commute Beneath the Bed: Floor-Borne Transit Vibration as a Cause of Sleep Fragmentation

## Project Summary

Environmental sleep research has focused primarily on light, temperature, and audible noise. Yet buildings also transmit low-frequency mechanical energy from rail lines, freight traffic, ventilation equipment, and late-night construction. These vibrations can reach a sleeper through the bed frame even when the associated sound is faint or masked. Building standards generally assess whether vibration is consciously perceptible, not whether repeated sub-perceptual events disturb sleeping physiology. This leaves a potentially modifiable source of sleep disruption largely unmeasured.

Our central hypothesis is that brief, floor-borne vibrations produce cortical and autonomic microarousals through somatosensory and vestibular pathways, independently of audible noise. We further hypothesize that event timing matters: vibrations arriving during stable non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep will be less disruptive than those occurring near spontaneous transitions in sleep depth. We will test these propositions through an integrated field, laboratory, and mitigation study in Lydon, a metropolitan area with varied combinations of surface rail, underground rail, and nighttime freight activity.

In a pilot study of 18 adults, we synchronized bedroom accelerometry with ambulatory polysomnography over three nights. Vibration events between 5 and 14 Hz were followed within 15 seconds by an EEG-defined microarousal 31% more often than matched vibration-free intervals. The association persisted after adjustment for A-weighted sound level, although the small sample did not permit separation of building, individual, and event-level effects. These findings establish feasibility and motivate the following aims.

**Aim 1: Determine whether naturally occurring floor vibration predicts sleep fragmentation in occupied bedrooms.** We will recruit 96 adults aged 20–45 years from 32 buildings spanning four transit-exposure zones. Each participant will complete 14 nights of measurement using a forehead EEG/EOG unit, ECG patch, under-mattress pressure sensor, and synchronized tri-axial accelerometers mounted on the floor slab and bed frame. Calibrated microphones will record sound-pressure levels without retaining intelligible audio. Indoor temperature, light, alcohol and caffeine use, exercise, bedtime, chronotype, and self-reported stress will be measured as covariates. A preregistered event-detection algorithm will identify transient vibration events and quantify their frequency, amplitude, dominant frequency, rise time, and transmission from floor to bed.

The primary outcome will be the probability of an EEG microarousal within 15 seconds of event onset compared with time-matched control windows from the same sleep stage and night. Secondary outcomes will include heart-rate acceleration, pulse-transit-time change, stage transition, awakening, and next-morning psychomotor vigilance. Hierarchical models will account for events nested within nights, participants, and buildings. Distributed-lag analyses will test the temporal specificity of responses, while interactions with sleep stage and phase of the slow-oscillation cycle will identify periods of heightened susceptibility. With an anticipated 80 evaluable participants after attrition, simulations based on pilot variance indicate greater than 80% power to detect an event-associated odds ratio of 1.20 for microarousal.

**Aim 2: Isolate the causal effect of vibration from the effects of concurrent sound.** Fifty-four participants from Aim 1, balanced across low and high field sensitivity, will complete four counterbalanced nights in the Somnus Environmental Suite. After an adaptation night, each participant will receive three randomized exposure conditions: floor-borne, transit-like vibration with minimal airborne sound; recorded transit sound delivered without measurable floor vibration; and a combined sound-plus-vibration condition. Sham events will be interspersed within every night. Vibration waveforms will be derived from field recordings but normalized to each participant’s evening detection threshold; most events will be delivered 3 dB below that threshold, with a smaller set at 3 dB above it to estimate dose-response functions. Sound-only events will be matched to the combined condition on perceived loudness during evening calibration.

Technicians scoring sleep will be blinded to event condition, and automated scoring will be followed by adjudication of uncertain epochs. The primary contrast will compare sub-threshold vibration events with sham events for microarousal probability. Sound-only and combined conditions will test whether mechanical and acoustic exposures act additively or interact. Event delivery will be stratified across N2, N3, and rapid eye movement sleep using real-time staging, with no more than six events per hour to limit habituation and preserve sleep architecture. Exploratory high-density EEG source estimates and heart-rate variability will characterize the sequence of cortical and autonomic responses. This experiment will establish whether vibration itself is sufficient to disturb sleep, rather than merely serving as a proxy for audible transit noise.

**Aim 3: Test a practical building-level mitigation strategy.** Forty-eight Aim 1 households with frequent vibration exposure will enter a randomized, two-period crossover trial of adaptive bed-foot isolators. The isolators use a passive elastomer core whose stiffness can be altered without changing bed height or appearance. Each household will receive three weeks of the attenuation setting and three weeks of a visually identical control setting, separated by a one-week washout. Floor and bed-frame accelerometry will verify whether the active setting reduces transmission in the prespecified 5–14 Hz band. Participants will complete ambulatory EEG on the first and final three nights of each period and wear an actigraphy device throughout.

The primary mitigation outcome will be within-participant change in microarousals per hour; secondary outcomes will include sleep efficiency, morning sleepiness, psychomotor vigilance, and perceived vibration. Analyses will follow intention-to-treat principles, with a per-protocol sensitivity analysis based on verified mechanical attenuation. We will also test whether benefit is concentrated among beds and floor systems with high baseline transmission ratios, providing an engineering rule for targeting future interventions.

Across aims, sex will be balanced at recruitment, analysis code and de-identified event-level data will be released, and primary outcomes and exclusion rules will be preregistered before data lock. Concordance among field associations, controlled exposures, and a mechanical intervention will provide unusually strong triangulation for an environmental sleep question. The project will produce exposure-response estimates, an open protocol for synchronized vibration and sleep measurement, and initial evidence on a low-cost mitigation approach. If the hypotheses are supported, the findings will broaden the concept of the nighttime soundscape to include mechanical energy that is felt imperfectly—or not consciously felt at all—while still fragmenting sleep.
